All the recent edits I've made to `main.js` were focused on tweaking visual and animation details: adjusting background color, material properties, ear geometry, key rotation dynamics, and numerous camera positions throughout the cutscene timeline. Each change was targeted to improve the look and feel of the scene based on the feedback loop we’ve been iterating through.

Now that these modifications are applied, the next logical step is to verify that they actually produce the intended visual results. Since the project uses a script `capture.mjs` to render a series of daily screenshots (the “dailies”) over a 60‑second real‑time run, I need to re‑run that capture process to generate fresh images reflecting the latest code changes. This will let me compare the new frames against the previous ones and confirm that the tweaks have the desired effect (e.g., the tin material looks better, the ear positioning is more natural, the camera follows are smoother, etc.).

The capture script is executed via Node.js from the project root, so I must change the working directory to the `wind-up-chase` folder and then invoke `node capture.mjs`. Because the capture can take up to a minute or more, I should give the command a generous timeout—say three minutes (180,000 ms)—to ensure it completes without being prematurely killed.

Thus, the appropriate next action is a PowerShell tool call that changes to the correct directory and runs the capture script with an adequate timeout. This will produce the updated dailies for me to review.
